exaggerated

/ig-ZAJ-uh-ray-tid/ — stress on ZAJ or AJ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something exaggerated is made to seem larger, more dramatic, or more extreme than it really is.

His exaggerated yawn made it clear he found the lecture boring.

Example

The comedian's exaggerated limp across the stage, with comic winces and theatrical groans, made the audience burst into laughter.

Exaggerated is precise because it means the limp was made bigger and more extreme than any real injury would be — the point was to distort reality for comic effect. Words like 'dramatic' just mean striking; exaggerated captures the distortion itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

theatrical: Theatrical means showy and dramatic, as if performed on a stage for an audience. Something exaggerated is stretched past the truth whether anyone is watching or not; something theatrical is aimed at watchers. A gesture can be theatrical without distorting any fact at all.

inflated: Inflated means puffed up beyond true size or worth, and it attaches to things that can be measured — inflated prices, inflated grades, an inflated ego. Exaggerated is the wider word for anything at all made to seem bigger or more extreme than it really is.

dramatic: Dramatic means striking, exciting, full of tension — and a dramatic thing can be perfectly real: a dramatic rescue actually happened that way. Exaggerated always means the reality has been stretched; the size or drama on display is more than the truth supports.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understated: expressed as less dramatic than it is

accurate: matching the facts exactly as they are

Where it sits · how far past the truth it goes — stated → overstated → embellished → exaggerated

stated vs. exaggerated: Stated is the neutral baseline far below exaggerated: a stated fact is simply reported as it is, while an exaggerated one is stretched beyond the truth.

overstated vs. exaggerated: Overstated is a step toward exaggerated: an overstated claim goes somewhat past the facts, while an exaggerated one blows them up dramatically.

embellished vs. exaggerated: Embellished comes just below exaggerated: an embellished story adds decorative details, while an exaggerated story inflates the whole picture beyond recognition.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: thoroughly, out (Latin)

Root — agger

Root — agger: heap, pile (Latin)

Suffix — -ate(d)

Suffix — -ate(d): to make (past form) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- ('thoroughly') + agger ('heap') + -ate literally meant 'to pile up thoroughly' — something exaggerated has details heaped on until it seems larger, more dramatic, or more extreme than it really is.

Use the root in a new word: exaggeration

Use the root in a new word: exaggeration: Saying you waited 'a million hours' for lunch is an exaggeration. Latin agger named a heap — Roman builders stacked earth into big mounds called aggers. An exaggeration stacks a story taller than life, and exaggerated describes the result.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Reach for exaggerated when something is made bigger, more dramatic, or more extreme than the truth — whether intentionally (for comic effect) or not. For something merely stated too strongly, 'overstated' works. For something that's genuinely large or dramatic, don't use exaggerated — just say 'large' or 'dramatic.'
